INTRODUCTION 
 1.1   INTRODUCTION 
Community Engagement is an essential aspect of holistic education. The course MS-299: Community 
Engagement (Mentoring School Students) is a 2-credit course introduced by Delhi Technological 
University to foster a sense of social responsibility among engineering undergraduates. The core 
philosophy of this course is to utilize the knowledge and skills of university students to mentor and 
guide school students, thereby bridging the gap between higher education and school-level 
understanding. 
 1.2   COURSE CONTEXT 
As per the guidelines issued by the Office of Dean (OEA), the engagement requires approximately 30 
hours of work spread across the academic year. The activities are designed to cover developmental 
stages, soft skills training, and specific mentoring topics such as academic guidance or career 
planning. 
 1.3   THE NEED FOR CAREER GUIDANCE 
For this project, I chose the specific domain of “Career and Future Planning” as outlined in the course 
syllabus deliverables. 
The 10th standard is a critical juncture in the Indian education system. Students are required to 
make a choice between Science, Commerce, and Humanities streams, a decision that significantly 
impacts their future professional lives. Often, students from underprivileged backgrounds or 
government schools lack access to proper counselling regarding the vast array of career options 
available today. 
 1.4   PROJECT LOCATION 
The mentoring sessions were conducted at STAR INSTITUTE OF COMMERCE, focusing on a group 
of students currently studying in Class 10. The goal was not just to teach, but to “handhold” them 
through the confusion of career selection.

UNDERSTANDING THE MENTEES (NEEDS ANALYSIS) 
 3.1   DEVELOPMENTAL STAGES OF MENTEES 
Before commencing the technical guidance, it was crucial to understand the psychological and 
emotional state of the students, as mandated by the “Understanding School Student” module of the 
syllabus. 
• Psychological State: The students are in the adolescent stage (15-16 years). They exhibited high 
energy but also significant anxiety regarding peer pressure and parental expectations. 
• Academic Challenges: Many students expressed a fear of Mathematics and Science. There was a 
prevalent myth that “only Science leads to success,” which needed to be addressed. 
• Socio-Economic Factors: A majority of the students come from backgrounds where access to 
professional career counselors is non-existent. Their knowledge of careers was limited to 
traditional roles like Doctor, Engineer, or Police Officer. 
 3.2   IDENTIFYING NEEDS 
Through an initial interaction and a simple show-of-hands survey, I identified the following needs: 
1. Lack of information about entrance exams (JEE, NEET, CUET). 
2. Confusion about the subject combinations available in Class 11. 
3. A need for role models to look up to.

One-on-one interaction to understand individual student interests

Self-Reflection (Who am I?)

PHASE 2 
Stream Selection (What 
should I choose?)

Science, Commerce, and

“easy” and “hard” streams. 
PHASE 3 
The Road Ahead (Where 
will I go?)

 4.2   TEACHING AIDS USED

“silly” questions without fear.

PHASE 1: IDENTIFYING INTERESTS & STRENGTHS 
 5.1   ACTIVITY OVERVIEW 
The first major module focused on “Identifying interests and strengths”. Many students choose 
streams based on what their friends are doing. The goal here was to promote independent thinking. 
 5.2   THE “MY DREAM CAREER” EXERCISE 
I asked every student to write down three careers they were curious about on a piece of paper. 
• Observation: 60% of the class wrote “Engineer” or “Doctor”. 
• Intervention: I asked them why. Many couldn’t answer. This opened the door for a discussion on 
aptitude. 
 5.3   CONNECTING SUBJECTS TO CAREERS 
I explained how current subjects translate to future careers: 
Good at debate/social science? 
→ 
Law, Journalism, Civil Services. 
Good at numbers/logic? 
→ 
Engineering, CA, Data Science. 
Good at biology/care? 
→ 
Medicine, Nursing, Psychology. 
This session helped students realize that every subject has a future value if pursued with passion.

PHASE 2: INTRODUCTION TO CAREER PATHWAYS 
 6.1   DECODING THE STREAMS 
This was the most technical part of the mentorship. I dedicated multiple hours to explaining the 
three major streams available after Class 10. 
A 
Science Stream 
(PCM/PCB) 
• I explained the rigor required for Physics, Chemistry, and 
Math/Biology. 
• We discussed engineering (B.Tech) and medical (MBBS) but also 
alternative options like Architecture, Merchant Navy, and 
Biotechnology. 
B 
Commerce Stream 
• I introduced them to Accountancy and Business Studies. 
• We discussed careers in Banking, Finance, Chartered Accountancy 
(CA), and Company Secretary (CS). 
C 
Humanities/Arts 
• I strongly advocated for the Arts stream, breaking the stigma that 
it is for “weak students.” 
• We discussed Psychology, Design, Mass Communication, and the 
Civil Services (UPSC).

Explaining the difference between 
Science, Commerce, and Humanities

PHASE 3: HIGHER EDUCATION & ENTRANCE EXAMS 
 7.1   ENTRANCE EXAMS 
As a B.Tech student at DTU, I was able to give them first-hand information about the Joint Entrance 
Examination (JEE). I explained the preparation process, the discipline required, and the rewards of 
getting into a top government college. 
We also briefly touched upon NEET for medical aspirants and CUET for central university admissions. 
 7.2   VOCATIONAL & NEW AGE CAREERS 
Aligned with the syllabus requirement to provide “Guidance on higher education and vocational 
training”, I spoke about: 
• Graphic Designing and Animation. 
• Coding and App Development (Introduction to the IT sector). 
• Hotel Management and Hospitality. 
 7.3   Q&A SESSION 
The final part of the interactions was an open 
house. 
Student Question: “Is Math compulsory for 
being a pilot?” 
My Answer: Yes, Physics and Math are 
usually required. 
Student Question: “Can I become an IAS 
officer if I take Science?” 
My Answer: Yes, you can appear for UPSC 
from any stream.

Resolving individual queries regarding entrance exams

MENTOR’S EXPERIENCE & IMPACT ASSESSMENT 
 8.1   RELATIONSHIP BUILDING 
Q: Do you think you have established a good relationship with your mentees? 
Yes. Initially, the students were shy, seeing me as a senior “teacher.” However, by using 
relatable examples and speaking in a mix of English and Hindi, I bridged the gap. By the third 
session, they were comfortable sharing their personal fears about exams. 
 8.2   LEARNING OUTCOMES 
Q: What do you think your mentee has learned from you during the program? 
The mentees have gained a structured understanding of the Indian education system. They 
learned that career choice should be a function of Aptitude + Interest, not just parental 
pressure. They now know the names of specific entrance exams and the subjects required for 
them. 
 8.3   SUCCESS STORY 
Q: What were some of the highlights for you? 
One specific success story is of a student named [Name, e.g., Rohan]. He was very good at 
drawing but was being forced into Non-Medical (Science). After our session on Design and 
Architecture, he realized he could pursue B.Arch. I guided him on the NATA exam. Seeing his 
relief and excitement was a highlight for me. 
 8.4   CHALLENGES 
There were questions I couldn’t answer immediately, specifically regarding the fee structures 
of private medical colleges. I noted these down, researched them, and provided the answers in 
the subsequent visit.

FEEDBACK & CONCLUSION

Group photo with the Mentees

9.1   FEEDBACK MECHANISM 
Feedback was collected based on the Annexure III template provided by the university. As part of the 
documentation, I have attached two forms: one form containing the names of all mentors and one 
form containing the names of all mentees. 
Summary of Mentee Feedback: 
• Average Interactions: Weekly interactions over the course of the semester. 
• Skills Listed by Mentees: Time Management, Exam Strategy, and Career Awareness. 
• General Remarks: Students appreciated the approachable nature of the sessions, noting that the 
“peer-to-peer” learning style made them feel more comfortable asking basic questions than they 
would in a formal classroom setting.

 9.2   CONCLUSION 
The MS-299 Community Engagement course has been a transformative experience. While 
the primary objective was to mentor the students regarding their future career paths, I found 
myself learning immense patience, empathy, and communication skills. 
Over the course of the required 30 hours, I believe I have successfully planted the seeds of 
ambition and clarity in these 10th-grade students. This project has reinforced my belief that 
education is not just about personal gain, but about lifting the community as we rise. The 
engagement allowed me to bridge the gap between school-level understanding and the 
reality of higher education. 
 9.3   FUTURE SCOPE 
I plan to stay in touch with these students digitally to help them when their actual board 
results are declared, ensuring the “handholding” process continues beyond the academic 
requirement of this course.
